analysis.title: The correlation multiverse – one index, many markets
key_insights: The S&P 500 index looks calm while single-stock risk stays active. The share of stock-return variation explained by the broad market factor (PC1) is close to the bottom of its post-2016 range.

Return-based clusters of S&P 500 stocks have risen from roughly 25 to 66 under SG's base specification, using 252-day rolling pairwise correlations and hierarchical clustering with average linkage and a fixed distance threshold.
Correlation within clusters remains strong, while correlation between clusters has fallen sharply. Index volatility is subdued because risk is localised and separate groups offset each other's moves.

Average within-cluster covariance per eligible pair has risen, while between-cluster covariance has stayed relatively flat. SG reads this as risk concentrating inside clusters instead of transmitting between them.
A single average correlation figure blends tightly co-moving pairs inside clusters with weakly related pairs across clusters, and describes neither well.
Return-based clusters show limited overlap with macro and fundamental groupings (low but positive ARI) and cut across the sector map. Sectors are a weak guide to which stocks currently move together.

Information Technology contains software, hardware and semiconductor stocks that have responded differently as the AI theme has developed. The overlap between cluster C3 and Information Technology is the exception, not the rule.

In-sample tests with 10,000 matched samples show portfolios diversified across return clusters have lower realised volatility and a better fifth-percentile return than portfolios diversified across sectors. Both use the same trailing 252-day window and equal weights.
The diversification benefit depends on the market staying fragmented. The main risk is a reconnection of groups that now move separately.

SG lists three signals for a reversal: commonality (rising PC1 and between-cluster correlation), topology (stronger links between clusters and a drop in cluster count) and intensity (higher single-name volatility with higher between-cluster correlation). No single signal is likely to be decisive.

sector_views.rationale: Sector contains software, hardware and semiconductor stocks that have moved differently during the AI theme, so the sector label is a weak guide to co-movement.

earnings_insights: The report cites earnings surprises as highly visible single-stock events but gives no specific EPS or revenue figures.
risk_factors: A reconnection of the currently separate clusters would remove the diversification benefit and lift index variance.
Results are in-sample, and single-stock volatility is not controlled in the portfolio simulations, so name selection feeds into the results.
Cluster count depends on the threshold, window and linkage choice. Sensitivity tests keep the broad rise in fragmentation but change the exact count.
vol_and_positioning: Index volatility is subdued while single-stock volatility stays active, because between-cluster correlation has fallen and moves across clusters cancel at index level.
PC1 explains close to the lowest share of S&P 500 variation since 2016.
Cluster-diversified portfolios show lower annualised realised volatility and better fifth-percentile returns than sector-diversified portfolios in SG's in-sample simulation.
Reconnection signals: rising PC1, rising between-cluster correlation, fewer clusters, and higher single-name volatility alongside higher between-cluster correlation.

tension_points.bull_case: Index volatility is subdued and cluster-diversified portfolios show lower realised volatility and a better left tail than sector-diversified ones.
tension_points.bear_case: The calm depends on clusters staying disconnected. Single-stock risk stays active, and a reconnection of groups would raise index variance and remove the diversification benefit.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rise in PC1 and between-cluster correlation, a collapse in cluster count, and higher single-name volatility alongside higher between-cluster correlation.
